KEY MESSAGE 1...

High pressure remains the main surface feature through the start
of the weekend, and the forecast area is clear and mild this
afternoon. Afternoon highs should reach the upper 70s to 
around 80 in the Metro Valley, southeast Ohio, and northeast 
Kentucky, and the mid 60s to lower 70s on the higher ridges of 
the Northeast Mountains. A dry layer is already present just 
above the boundary layer. Mixing into that layer should pull 
afternoon dewpoints down into the 40s to around 50 by late day,
several degrees below central guidance, which holds the mid 
50s. Minimum relative humidity this afternoon should fall into 
the 30 to 45 percent range in the lowlands. That is dry for 
early October, but wind is too light and the forest floor
remains generally sheltered by trees in nearly full leaf for
much of a fire weather concern. Yesterday afternoon 10 hour 
fuel moisture at several RAWS sites fell to around 7 to 11 
percent, then recovered above 18 percent overnight with no 
rainfall, so fine dead fuels are drying each afternoon and 
recovering at night. 

A dry cold front crosses from northwest to southeast late
tonight into Thursday morning. Parent low pressure stays well
north, over James Bay and Quebec, and the boundary has
essentially no moisture with it. The sensible change is the 
wind shift to northwest and a deeper push of dry air. 

Thursday and Friday afternoons look several degrees drier than
raw central guidance dewpoints. MOS consensus drops Charleston 
dewpoints into the upper 30s to mid 40s behind the front, and 
HRRR already mixes Huntington and the northeast Kentucky sites 
into the upper 30s to around 40 by late this afternoon. 
Afternoon highs Thursday should still reach the upper 70s to 
around 80 in the lowlands and the upper 60s to mid 70s in the 
higher terrain, then the mid to upper 70s Friday, with minimum 
relative humidity again near 30 to 40 percent. Northwest wind 
Thursday afternoon will be 10 to 15 mph, with gusts 20 to 30 mph
on the more exposed ridges of the Northeast Mountains. 

Friday morning should be the chilliest of this stretch of the
forecast, and central guidance looks too warm in the valleys as
is typical in these setups. The forecast leans toward the 
cooler MOS solution in areas subject to cold air drainage away 
from major rivers: mid 30s to around 40 in the sheltered 
mountain valleys, and the mid 40s in the Metro Valley and along 
the major rivers. Where the temperature and dewpoint both settle
in the mid 30s under a clear sky and calm wind, patchy frost is
possible Friday morning, mainly in the Northeast Mountains and 
colder hollows. Ridgetops will stay milder than the valleys. A 
similar, slightly less cold ridge/valley split is possible 
Saturday morning before clouds thicken.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Tropical Storm Isaias was centered just north of the Bay of
Campeche moving east-northeast at 7KTs, with maximum sustained 
wind of 40KTs and a central pressure near 1000 mb as of the 10AM
NHC forecast. The official forecast takes it to hurricane 
strength on Thursday, toward the northern Gulf Coast on Friday, 
inland as a weakening tropical storm Saturday morning, and to a 
depression near the lower Ohio Valley by early Sunday. 

The likely local outcome is a surge of tropical moisture
beginning as early as Saturday afternoon, first in the southern
coalfields and northeast Kentucky, then spreading across the
rest of the area Saturday night. Rain should persist through at
least late Sunday night as that moisture interacts with an
approaching mid-latitude trough. A general 1 to 2 inches is
expected with the 48 hr total interquartile range around those
values. A farther east or faster remnant would favor that lower
end and would keep the better low-level shear east of the 
forecast area. A slower or farther west track would hold the 
circulation over the Ohio Valley longer on Sunday and could push
local totals above 2 inches, especially if heavier cores train.

The most efficient rain looks to be late Sunday morning into
Sunday afternoon. Forecast profiles at Charleston and Beckley 
for Sunday morning are nearly saturated from the surface through
H700, with the freezing level and wet-bulb zero both near 12000
to 14000 ft. That is a deep warm-cloud layer. Buoyancy looks 
tall but skinny, extending up toward H400, which favors 
efficient warm-rain processes. 

Isolated poor-drainage flooding and quick rises on small 
streams are possible if a heavier band stalls. Southeast flow 
ahead of the remnant low can also wring out a bit more on 
windward eastern slopes and, by isentropic descent, locally cut 
totals on the immediate lee side of the higher ridges. Rain
tapers from west to east Sunday night into Monday as the 
remnant low pulls toward the Atlantic.

Sunday. Instability should be largely elevated, which keeps the
